title: Real-time probing of quadrupolar contributions to the absorption cross section of non-periodic systems
authors: Anvar Khujakulov, Michele Guerrini, Carlo Andrea Rozzi, Caterina Cocchi
abstract: The non-perturbative evaluation of multipolar cross sections is essential for probing atomic and molecular responses to spatially inhomogeneous electric fields characteristic of nanoscale environments where the conventional dipole approximation breaks down. Taking the hydrogen atom as an analytical and numerical benchmark, we map in real time quadrupole interactions driven by instantaneous electric field gradients. Our study explores two distinct interaction regimes. Under a uniform field, quadrupolar responses are activated by multi-step dipole transitions, responsible for sub-1~eV excited-state absorption. Conversely, under pure spatial gradients, the weak-field response is dominated by the single-photon $1s \to 3d$ quadrupole resonance at 12.1~eV, while strong gradients induce low-energy stimulated emission via transiently driven coherent populations. This dynamical analysis is complemented by a rigorous evaluation of the symmetry aspects of the quadrupole response and the applied electric field. This methodology establishes the theoretical and computational foundation for future non-perturbative multipole simulations of molecules and nanostructures in the near-field regime.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical method to calculate the full multipolar cross section by incorporating quadrupole contributions, moving beyond the standard dipole approximation for atomic response. Using the hydrogen atom as a benchmark, the authors simulate real-time electron dynamics under varying electric field gradients. The results show that strong fields activate distinct low-energy spectral features due to these higher-order coupling mechanisms.
main_problem: The study addresses the necessity of going beyond the dipole approximation to probe multipolar cross sections, specifically quadrupolar contributions, when analyzing atomic and molecular responses in highly inhomogeneous electric fields.
main_result: The research demonstrates that quadrupole interactions become crucial under strong gradients or intense fields, leading to distinct spectral features such as low-energy sub-1 eV absorption or stimulated emission peaks not predicted by dipole theory alone.
method: The authors employ real-time, non-perturbative simulations using the Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation (TDSE) framework, extending established methods like those in Octopus code.
model_or_system: The primary benchmark system is the hydrogen atom, treated as a one-electron system. The analysis involves modeling electron dynamics under an interaction Hamiltonian containing both dipole and quadrupole terms derived from field gradients.
key_observables: Photo-absorption cross section ($\sigma_{	ext{tot}}(\omega)$), quadrupole expectation value ($\Omega_{qd}(t)$), and the ratio of multipolar contributions ($\sigma_{qd}/\sigma_d$).
important_parameters: Field regimes include weak, linear response (dipole dominated) versus strong, nonlinear response (quadrupole effects become prominent); energy scales range from sub-1 eV to 12.1 eV.
main_assumptions: The methodology relies on the multipolar expansion for classification but uses non-perturbative real-time propagation; limitations include potential discrepancies between TDSE and finite-grid solvers like Octopus.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how the total cross section changes across different field regimes (linear vs. nonlinear), showing resonance depletion and the emergence of low-energy features attributable to higher-order multipole coupling.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes four distinct excitation regimes (WD, SD, WD+WQ, SD+SQ) using the hydrogen atom benchmark, building a theoretical foundation for non-perturbative multipole simulations in near-field environments.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous computational framework for understanding how higher-order field interactions govern light absorption and emission in nanoscale or molecular settings where simple dipole approximations fail. It is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems dynamics.
